title: Choosing a Model: families, sizes & tradeoffs
summary: Not every agent step needs your biggest model. Models come in families (frontier vs small/open) and sizes, and each choice trades quality against latency and cost. The skill is matching the model to the step — reserving frontier reasoning for hard planning and routing routine steps to a small, cheap model — and proving the choice with evals rather than vibes.

subtopics.title: Families and sizes: frontier vs small vs open
subtopics.explanation: Providers ship a family of models at different sizes: large 'frontier' models with the strongest reasoning, mid and small models that are faster and cheaper, and open-weight models you can self-host. A bigger model isn't strictly better for every step — it's better at hard reasoning but wastes money on trivial ones. Knowing the size ladder is the starting point for matching a model to each part of your agent.
subtopics.example:
# a rough size ladder, provider-agnostic
MODELS = {
    "frontier": {"quality": 5, "speed": 2, "cost": 5},  # hard reasoning
    "mid":      {"quality": 4, "speed": 3, "cost": 3},  # general purpose
    "small":    {"quality": 3, "speed": 5, "cost": 1},  # cheap & fast
}

def pick(need_reasoning: bool) -> str:
    # reserve the frontier tier for genuinely hard steps
    return "frontier" if need_reasoning else "small"

print(pick(need_reasoning=False))  # small
# choosing the size is the first tradeoff you make in any agent

subtopics.title: The quality / latency / cost triangle
subtopics.explanation: Every model choice moves three dials at once: answer quality, response latency, and dollar cost. Frontier models raise quality but are slower and pricier per token; small models flip that. You rarely maximize all three, so you decide which the current step actually needs — a user-facing autocomplete cares about latency, a one-off analysis cares about quality. Seeing the choice as a triangle keeps you from reflexively reaching for the most expensive option.

subtopics.title: Context window is a hard budget, not a suggestion
subtopics.explanation: Each model has a maximum context window — the total tokens of system prompt, tools, history, and the current input it can see at once. Exceed it and the call errors or silently truncates. A larger window costs more per call and often runs slower, so 'just use the biggest window' is not free. Picking a model means checking its window against how much history and tool output your agent realistically accumulates.
subtopics.example:
def fits(prompt_tokens: int, window: int) -> bool:
    # leave headroom for the model's own output
    reserve_for_output = 2000
    return prompt_tokens + reserve_for_output <= window

# a long agent run with lots of tool results
history_tokens = 90_000
print(fits(history_tokens, window=128_000))  # True
print(fits(history_tokens, window=32_000))   # False -> pick a bigger window or trim
# the window is a ceiling you must design your agent to stay under

subtopics.title: Tool-use and structured-output support vary by model
subtopics.explanation: Agents lean on two model capabilities: reliable tool/function calling and constrained structured output. Not every model — especially smaller or older open ones — supports these well; some emit malformed tool calls or ignore JSON schemas under pressure. Before adopting a model, confirm it does native tool calling and structured outputs at the reliability your loop needs, because a cheap model that botches tool calls costs you more in retries than it saves.

subtopics.title: Routing, fallback, and evaluating before you commit
subtopics.explanation: Mature agents don't pick one model forever — they route each step to the cheapest model that can handle it and fall back to a stronger one when the cheap answer fails a check. But routing rules are guesses until you measure: run the candidate models against a small eval set of your real tasks and compare quality and cost. Choosing a model is an empirical decision, so evals-before-commit is what turns 'I think it's good enough' into evidence.

foundations.overview: Choosing a model for an agent is a per-step engineering decision, not a one-time brand choice. Models arrive in families and sizes: large frontier models with the strongest reasoning, cheaper and faster mid/small models, and open-weight models you can host yourself. Each size trades quality against latency and cost — the three dials you can't max simultaneously. On top of size you must check practical constraints: the context window is a hard token ceiling, and agentic features like reliable tool calling and structured output are not uniform across models. The mature pattern is to route each step to the cheapest model that can do the job and fall back to a stronger one when a check fails. Crucially, every one of these choices is empirical: you validate candidate models on a small eval set of your real tasks before committing, so 'good enough' is backed by numbers rather than intuition.
foundations.formalDefinition: Model selection is the process of assigning, per agent step, a model from an available set — characterized by family (frontier/small/open), parameter size, context window, and capability support (tool calling, structured output) — that satisfies the step's quality requirement at acceptable latency and cost, optionally via a routing policy with fallback, and justified by evaluation on representative tasks.
foundations.whyItMatters: In an agent loop the same model may be called dozens of times, so the choice multiplies: a needlessly large model inflates cost and latency on every iteration, while a too-small one causes failed tool calls and retries that cost even more. Getting the match right per step is one of the highest-leverage decisions in agent design.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of your models as a team with different pay grades: a senior specialist (frontier) for the hard, ambiguous calls, and fast junior staff (small models) for routine work. You wouldn't put your most expensive expert on every trivial task, and you wouldn't hand a critical judgment to a junior — you route the work by difficulty and keep the senior on call as backup.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Coding agents use a strong model for planning and a cheaper one for boilerplate edits; support agents classify intent with a small model and escalate hard cases to a frontier one; RAG pipelines embed and rank with tiny models and only synthesize the final answer with a large one; data agents route simple SQL to a small model and complex multi-join reasoning to a bigger one.
commonUseCases: Routing cheap steps to small models, hard steps to frontier
Fallback to a stronger model when a quality check fails
Choosing a window that fits a long agent run's history

commonMisconceptions.myth: The biggest model is always the best choice.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's best at hard reasoning but wastes cost and latency on trivial steps, and its large context window is not free. The right model is the cheapest one that reliably passes the step's quality bar.

commonMisconceptions.myth: All models support tool calling and structured output equally.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Support and reliability vary a lot, especially for smaller or older open models. A model that botches tool calls triggers retries that erase any price savings — verify the capability, not just the price.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can pick a model by reputation or benchmark leaderboards alone.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Public benchmarks rarely match your task distribution. You have to eval candidate models on a small set of your real tasks, because 'good on paper' often isn't 'good on my data'.

foundations.performanceImpact: Because an agent re-invokes the model each loop iteration, model size drives both per-call latency and total run cost multiplicatively; routing routine steps to a small model can cut a run's cost by an order of magnitude, while an under-capable model raises the retry rate and can end up slower and more expensive than a larger one.

candidates.title: Small / fast
candidates.desc: Cheap, low-latency, great for high-volume classify/extract/route tasks.

candidates.title: Mid-tier
candidates.desc: The pragmatic default — solid reasoning at reasonable cost for mixed workloads.

candidates.title: Frontier
candidates.desc: Top reasoning and reliability for hard, multi-step, low-error-tolerance work.

questions.q: Is the task simple and high-volume (classify, extract, route)?
Does it need deep reasoning or long multi-step planning?
Is cost/latency at scale the top constraint?
Must outputs be top quality with few errors tolerated?
Is it a broad general task of mixed difficulty?

checkpoints.prompt: An agent step just formats a validated record into a fixed JSON shape. Which model tier is usually the right choice?
options: Always the frontier model for safety
A small, cheap model — the step needs little reasoning
Whichever model has the largest context window
It doesn't matter; all tiers cost the same
checkpoints.explanation: Formatting a known record needs almost no reasoning, so a small fast model handles it at a fraction of the cost. Reserve the frontier tier for genuinely hard steps; blindly using it everywhere inflates cost and latency across the whole loop.

checkpoints.code:
def fits(prompt_tokens, window, reserve=2000):
    return prompt_tokens + reserve <= window

print(fits(90_000, 128_000))
print(fits(90_000, 32_000))
checkpoints.explanation: 90,000 + 2,000 = 92,000 fits within 128,000 (True) but exceeds 32,000 (False). The context window is a hard ceiling you must design the agent's history to stay under, reserving headroom for the model's own output.

checkpoints.prompt: Why is a cheap model that frequently produces malformed tool calls often a bad choice for an agent, even though its per-token price is low?
options: Cheap models are always lower quality by definition
Each malformed call triggers retries (extra full calls), so total cost and latency can exceed a larger, reliable model
Tool calling is not needed in agents
The provider bans cheap models from tool use
checkpoints.explanation: In an agent loop, a botched tool call means a retry — another full model call plus latency. Enough retries erase the price savings, so capability and reliability, not just per-token price, must drive the choice.

keyTakeaways: Models come in families and sizes; match the tier to each step's difficulty rather than using one model everywhere.
Every choice trades quality against latency and cost — optimize for the dial the step actually cares about.
The context window is a hard token ceiling; check it against your agent's realistic history plus output headroom.
Verify tool-calling and structured-output reliability, because a model that botches them costs more in retries than it saves.
Route cheap steps to small models with fallback to stronger ones, and prove the routing rule with evals on your real tasks before committing.
